name: Ivan Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead an electricity-company crew building new power connections around the expanding north edge of town. My two-year technical diploma helps with the drawings, and years of trench work tell me where the drawings are wrong. I like seeing a new street lit; waiting for a developer to move a fence wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how much AI do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs a small childcare service, and our children are grown and paying their own bills. My lineworker pay is around the usual level, we have about four months of expenses saved and some other utility crews work nearby. Retirement is in sight but not dated, and I use AI daily for materials and job order before checking the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the connection crew the AI excitement was larger than the change, though my daily materials check still helps. A worker has to set the pole and test the new power line before a house gets electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead shifts look steady and my partner's childcare work keeps bringing in wages. We have around four months of expenses saved, so I can keep earning while we work out a retirement date rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading new housing connections and use the AI materials list I already run. Before ordering cable, I'll compare its length with the measured trench route and the approved drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, a little entertained that a useful list survived the big claims. I would still like the apprentices to learn a tape measure before a phone shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the material list miss something real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the list missed a bend around a drainage culvert, so we measured the route again. The AI cable order was tidy and short; the trench was real and longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a mild AI future change your retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep paying the usual bills and leave the savings account for emergencies. My partner and I will still review the retirement figures in winter, because our exit date must fit the household.

say: **AI material lists** can save time, but crews still measure and build new power connections.
**Apprentice measurements** matter before any cable is ordered.
think: My **lead lineworker wage** and partner's childcare income look steady.
Our **four-month reserve** allows a careful retirement review without an invented exit date.
do: **Keep** leading new housing connections with the existing crew.
**Check** AI cable lists against measured trenches and approved drawings.
feel: **Calm** about pay, amused by the smaller useful tool.
S0.quote: The AI cable order was tidy and short; the trench was real and longer.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily** for materials yet checks the actual trench and drawing measurements.
Both jobs and a **four-month cushion** make the plateau financially manageable.

steps.text: Keep leading new housing connections and checking cable measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can buy fittings and book crews before robots can dig and string a new connection. If the planner gives us a full day of work in six hours, somebody must correct it before a crew gets blamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical work still has plenty of demand, but a faster schedule could quietly take away paid travel time. Four months saved would cover a short gap, not years of smaller pay packets as I get nearer retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll test the approved AI schedule on three completed connection jobs and compare planned travel with what the crew actually logged. If the tool passes, I'll learn its editing controls on paid time and keep a record of travel hours for the next six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible pay cut through hours, though I expect to keep building lines. A six-hour AI schedule will not make our power-line crew's eight-hour drive and build disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the supervisor about wrong travel time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send the supervisor the old job sheets with the road closures marked. A route that saves time on a screen may add an hour to the crew's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the six-month travel pay with the same season before the planner. If it drops, I'll ask the company to put the actual travel back on the roster.

say: **AI scheduling** should use actual travel times before assigning new line connections.
**Robots** will reach physical building later than software reaches buying and booking.
think: My **construction role** looks secure, but paid travel hours could shrink.
Four months of **savings** cannot make a continuing pay reduction harmless before retirement.
do: **Test** approved AI schedules on three completed connection jobs.
**Learn** planner editing controls on paid time if the test succeeds.
**Track** travel pay for six months after the new schedule starts.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic travel-pay loss, with a way to test it.
S1.quote: A six-hour AI schedule will not make our power-line crew's eight-hour drive and build disappear.
fieldNote: He tests **actual travel time** on completed connection jobs rather than accepting new schedule estimates.
Potential **hour loss** before retirement makes him anxious despite his strong technical standing.

steps.text: Test approved AI schedule on three completed connections
Learn planner editing controls on paid time if test succeeds
Track six months of travel pay after new schedule begins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 changes buying and planning first, with capable installation robots around 2031. We should ask the company how many people it will pay to connect new streets after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 when robots can do the hands-on build, and I might still need the wage. My partner's childcare hours are physical, but our four-month reserve will not cover a long loss of my line pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask management for the 2028 planning and 2031 field staffing figures. I'll apply for a paid installation-robot pilot if it offers normal wages and real stop controls, and my partner and I will compare our retirement income with household bills before setting any date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible crew cuts, but I have skills and some nearby utilities to contact. I don't assume the pilot is a guaranteed new post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children that we are asking about shifts and savings, not calling for help. They have their own expenses, and I want a plan based on our two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the robot pilot real work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd operate the robot's stop control on a supervised connection job at my normal wage. A fence-side robot demonstration cannot replace the lineworker wage that pays our bills.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches buying and plans before installation robots around 2031.
The company should publish **paid field crew counts** for new connections.
think: At about **63**, I may still need line wages when robots arrive.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot bridge a long loss of my pay.
do: **Ask** company for 2028 planning and 2031 field staffing figures.
**Join** paid robot pilot if normal wages and real stop controls are offered.
**Compare** retirement income with household bills before setting an exit date.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible field-crew cut, with work and local options.
S2.quote: A fence-side robot demonstration cannot replace the lineworker wage that pays our bills.
fieldNote: His pilot means **operating controls**, not passive observation.
Retirement cost review is **information gathering**, with no early departure decided.
The **2031 robot date** catches him near 63, possibly before he can afford to leave.

steps.text: Ask company for 2028 plans and 2031 field staffing
Join paid installation robot pilot if normal wage and controls offered
Compare retirement income with household bills before exit date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 will change the plans, then capable field robots around 2034 could build the lines. Five years lets the company test them and gives my family time to work out when I can leave full shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66 I might prefer a paid quality-checking job to another long climb, if such a job exists. I cannot spend a title or an occasional lesson; a household bill needs real wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll run the approved AI materials checker on five old connection drawings and record where it misses site changes. If a company-paid robot controls course opens after a field trial with a posted quality-checker role, I'll enrol while keeping my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible field-hour cuts before retirement is affordable, with more time to test the new work. I am not buying a course just because an advert promises a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you mark on the old drawings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark each changed trench, cable size and delivery point on the five drawings. A planner that gets the old jobs wrong has no place deciding tomorrow's connection materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before enrolling in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A line-robot course without a posted wage is just a new certificate beside my old one. I'd enrol only for paid hours, hands-on controls and a posted job that covers our bills.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes connection plans before field robots around 2034.
A **paid quality-checker post** is a possible later role only if advertised with real wages.
think: At about **66**, I may want lighter paid work if retirement is not affordable.
No **checker job** has been offered, so a training title cannot pay our bills.
do: **Test** approved AI materials checker on five completed connection drawings.
**Enrol** in paid robot controls course if field trial and posted checker role follow.
feel: **Anxious** about possible construction-hour cuts before retirement is affordable.
S3.quote: A line-robot course without a posted wage is just a new certificate beside my old one.
fieldNote: He uses **five old jobs** as an evidence test before trusting planning AI.
Course enrolment requires **company funding**, field practice and a posted adequate-wage role.

steps.text: Test approved AI checker on five completed connection drawings
Enrol in company-paid robot course if field trial and paid checker role offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 changes the drawings first, and capable installation robots around 2039 arrive when I would be about 71. I hope to be off regular construction shifts then, if our retirement budget works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer horizon is easier for my own wage, but four months saved is not a final retirement plan. My partner and I need actual monthly figures before I choose a leaving date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year we'll review our retirement statements, house costs and any remaining debt, then set a monthly target. I'll keep my line safety tickets current and pass the tricky connection drawings to a younger crew member before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the robot timetable, careful about money. I want to stop work because we can afford it, not because someone switched on a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown son to teach a new worker why the drawing can miss a drain, rather than simply showing them an AI answer. An AI drawing can miss the drain that my power-line crew finds with muddy boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a proper drawing handover involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit with a younger worker over the culvert drawings and walk the route once. Handing over a file without the ground check would leave the next crew with my old mistakes.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes plans before 2039 robots can build connections.
**Ground checks** should pass to younger crews before older lineworkers leave.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be off construction shifts if retirement figures work.
Our **four-month reserve** alone does not set an affordable leaving date.
do: **Review** retirement statements and house costs with partner this year.
**Keep** line safety tickets current while leading connections.
**Hand** culvert drawings to younger crew member with an on-site walk.
feel: **Calm** about late robots, attentive to household finances.
S4.quote: An AI drawing can miss the drain that my power-line crew finds with muddy boots.
fieldNote: He expects 2039 robots **after hoped-for work**, conditional on retirement figures.
The handover includes an **on-site walk** for the younger worker, not just files or an abstract lesson.

steps.text: Review retirement statements and house costs with partner this year
Keep line safety tickets current while leading connections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because installation robots around 2031 could cut shifts when I am about 63 and may still need line wages. A real crew forecast and a paid controls path tied to a job would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the trench before the company accepts a machine's cable length. My phone gives a cable answer fast; my apprentice still has to measure the power-line trench. I want that check paid for after I leave the crew.

headlineQuote: My phone gives a cable answer fast; my apprentice still has to measure the power-line trench.
portrait: **Ivan**, 58, leads new power connections using a two-year technical diploma and years of site experience.
He uses **AI daily** for materials but checks generated cable lengths against real trenches.
His **typical pay**, childcare-service partner, four-month reserve and some nearby utility jobs leave retirement timing open.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about wages at 63; more time lets him test paid checking work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring installation robots around 2031 while his retirement budget is still unresolved.
whatWouldHelp: A real **crew forecast** and paid robot-controls path tied to a posted job would help.
